attempt: Water that appears half an hour after a load and smells foul is drain water getting back into the tub, not fresh water: the usual causes are a drain hose set too low (water siphons back), a failed check valve or drain-pump seal, or a leaking door bellow (which would give fresh water). Check the drain hose height against the manual (it must rise to the recommended height before turning down), run a drain-only cycle and watch for seep-back, and inspect the bellows. Foul smell means the drain side; clean-smelling water means the door seal.

Stuck full of water before the rinse cycle, fixable only by finding a knob sweet spot, points to an intermittent electrical contact in the timer/cycle switch or its knob, or a lid switch the machine does not see. Drain the tub first (emergency drain or a hose lowered to floor level), then check the lid switch for a click. If the machine only advances when the knob is wiggled, the timer or the knob's wiring pads are the fault; on an Ultimate Care II the timer is the common wear item for exactly this symptom.

Slow dispenser flow immediately after a filter change is usually an air lock in the filter housing, a filter that was not flushed, a partially closed saddle valve, or a wrong/clogged filter. Dispense two to three gallons to clear air, confirm the saddle valve is fully open, and check the seat seal for the leak seen at the housing. If flow stays slow after several gallons, the filter is clogged or the wrong part for that GE model.

A rotting-garbage smell with standing water under the filter assembly means debris in the sump or a partially blocked drain: a clean filter does not clean the sump strainer or the drain. Remove the lower filter and sump cover, clear the strainer and the drain of food, check the drain hose for a clog, and run a hot empty cycle with a dishwasher cleaner. If the standing water is deep rather than the usual shallow puddle, the drain pump or its check valve is the fault.

A washer that trips a GFCI mid-cycle has a ground fault: most often water from a leaking hose, pump seal, or inlet valve reaching a live part, or (on heated models) a cracked heating element grounding through the water. Dry the machine, check hoses and the pump area for leaks, and briefly test on a non-GFCI outlet to confirm the fault is in the machine rather than the outlet. Do not bypass the GFCI; a machine that trips it is unsafe until the leak is found.

The black film on the axle is degraded lubricant or the nylon roller surface stripping, and these rollers are plain nylon bushings that are not meant to hold grease: oil and grease migrate and gum the bushing. Clean the axles and rollers of all old lubricant, dry thoroughly, and run them dry (nylon is self-lubricating) or with a silicone lubricant sparingly. Replace any roller with a flat spot or a crack. If the film reappears, the roller material itself is failing and the rollers should be replaced, not re-lubricated.

Condensation that drips in a long, upward vent run in hot humid weather is the exhaust cooling and condensing in the attic section, then running back. Insulate the vent where it passes through the attic, keep the run as short and straight as the installation allows, and make sure the roof cap has a working damper. A crushed or lint-choked duct makes it worse. If the dryer is gas, have the installation checked for combustion safety before continuing to use it.

After a fridge is left open all day, a cold freezer with a warm fridge points to cold air not reaching the fridge: the evaporator fan (it only runs in some cycles), a blocked vent between the compartments, or a defrost problem — or it may simply need 24 hours to recover. Listen for the fan whenever the compressor runs; if it never runs while the freezer is cold, the fan or its damper is the fault. Clear the vent and give it overnight before replacing anything.

Orange flames on every gas appliance at once, with normal measured pressure, is a supply-side problem, not an appliance problem: pressure can be right while the gas itself is wrong, or a regulator is still faulty, or air is being drawn into the line. Stop using the appliances (soot means incomplete combustion and a CO risk) and ask the gas company specifically for a gas-quality analysis, a regulator inspection, and a leak-down test with the system pressurized and isolated. Appliance-level fixes cannot address a problem every appliance shares.

The beeper works from the buttons but the timer-end signal does not sound, so the speaker is good and the fault is in the end-of-cycle signal path: a control setting (many Whirlpool ovens have a signal/sound on-off option) or the timer buzzer circuit. Check the manual for a sound or signal setting first, then reset the control (breaker off for one to two minutes). If the setting is on and the reset does not restore the end-of-cycle beep, the buzzer or its drive on the control board has failed.

Water heard under the drum after the spin cycle, with a mildew smell, is incomplete draining: a clogged drain pump, a kinked drain hose, or a too-low standpipe. If the water is fresh-smelling instead, a leaking inlet valve dribbles water in continuously while the machine does not fully drain. Check the drain hose for clogs and the standpipe height, run a drain-only cycle and watch the pump, and treat the smell with a cleaner once the drain is clear.

Two dishwashers in a row that do not drain, with the old one's hose and trap already cleaned, points to the household drain, not the machines: a clogged shared drain line, a blocked air gap, or a drain hose without the required high loop (which lets the machine siphon). Run the drain hose into a bucket: if the machine pumps freely into the bucket, the machine is fine and the shared drain line or air gap is the blockage; if it does not pump, the pump or its check valve is the fault.

White filaments in fridge water right after a filter change are usually mineral sediment stirred up by the new filter's first flow, or carbon fines from a filter that was not flushed. Run two to four gallons through the dispenser to flush it. If the filaments persist after flushing, the supply lines are shedding scale (common after plumbing work) and the line should be flushed at the supply; a sediment filter at the supply is the durable fix. White and hard means scale; black means carbon fines.

Out-of-balance with the lightest loads, banging, and repeated repositioning on a front-loader points to worn suspension shocks, tub bearings, or a leveling problem: worn shocks let the tub slam at spin even with small loads. Re-level the machine first (every foot should resist rocking with the door open), confirm no shipping bolts remain, and push the tub: it should resist, not swing. If leveling does not fix it, the shock absorbers or bearings need replacement; the service manual's balance test will confirm which.

Ice that builds in the vent between freezer and fridge until it blocks airflow is the defrost system not clearing the evaporator, or humid air leaking past a door gasket. Defrost the vent fully (low heat, carefully, since the structure is foam), then check the freezer gasket with a dollar-bill test. If ice returns within days of a full defrost, the defrost heater, defrost thermostat, or defrost timer is the fault; if it returns slowly over weeks, the gasket is the leak.

A spin-cycle noise that starts when the water is gone, without grinding or shaking, is most consistent with worn tub bearings or a worn spin tube: bearing noise is load-dependent and loudest when the empty tub spins fast. Open the cabinet and spin the tub by hand: a rumble that worsens with speed is the bearing; also inspect the belt and pulley for wear. If it is the bearings, continued use wears the spin tube and outer tub, so repair now rather than later.

An intermittent breaker trip on a ten-year-old fridge in hot weather is most often the compressor start relay or overload (tripping on start, especially in heat), or a grounded winding from a damp connection after defrost. Watch the timing: a trip within seconds of the compressor starting points to the start relay; a trip after running points to the compressor or a grounded winding. Clean the condenser coils; an electrician can megger the winding to ground.

Sides that are hot to 105F with loud running, when the machine used to run cool and quiet, is a change, and the technician's 'that is how it works' only holds for a clean machine: the usual cause is clogged condenser coils, then a failed condenser fan, then a compressor working too hard (low charge or wear). Clean the coils first and listen for the condenser fan; if coils and fan are clean and it still runs hot and loud, a service call for the compressor or charge is warranted.

A detergent cup that never opens is usually the wax motor (the small cylinder that pops the cup) or a stuck, clogged cup — not the detergent brand. Check the cup for clogs and free movement by hand; if it moves freely but still will not pop during a cycle, the wax motor or its wiring is the fault, and it is a cheap, accessible part on most machines. Hot water and rinse aid will not fix a cup that never opens.

The evidence in the question points to a ground fault from moisture: the ground wire reading 'all over the place' to the frame means damaged insulation or a chafed wire, and it began at defrost, when water enters connections. Leave the machine off and open for 24 hours to dry fully, then re-test. Inspect the ground wire's insulation and any wire routing near the frame or compressor for chafing, and ohm each wire to the frame one at a time. A machine that trips only when the ground is connected has a wire-to-frame fault and should not run until it is found.

Agitates but will not spin, with the coupler, pump, and lid switch verified, points to the clutch and brake assembly (the clutch engages spin only after the timer advances) or the timer never reaching spin. First confirm the timer actually advances to the spin position; if it does and the tub still does not spin, the clutch or brake is the fault — a common wear item on the Kenmore 80 series. The agitator being stoppable by hand during spin is consistent with the transmission not engaging spin.

A microwave that trips the breaker exactly when the door opens mid-heat points to a door interlock switch arcing or shorting as it changes state, or a grounding fault in the door harness. Stop using it, check the door hooks and the door's alignment against the switch actuators (a misaligned door makes a switch bounce), and expect to replace the interlock switches. Do not run it with a door switch defeated.

A power cord that warms near the plug end and is more pliable there localizes the fault: a damaged cord at the strain relief, or a loose or corroded plug-to-outlet contact. Stop using it, check the cord entry for a cracked strain relief and the prongs for corrosion, and feel whether the outlet itself is warm (a worn outlet is the other cause). A heater draws its full load, so a poor connection heats up; the cord or the outlet must be replaced before use.

On many stoves the igniters share one ignition module wired so that all of them spark while any burner calls for ignition, so all five sparking while one lights is typical behavior — the abnormal version is sparking that continues after the burner lights. Watch whether the sparking stops the moment the burner catches: if it stops and the burner lights reliably, this is normal; if it continues, one igniter's switch is shorted and should be replaced.

A smell that appears only in fan mode after cooling, fades in about two minutes, and disappears when cooling resumes is the evaporator: in AC mode the coil is cold and dry; in fan mode it warms, and the moisture on it mildews or the condensate pan sours. Run fan mode with the vent open to dry the coil, clean the filter and the condensate pan, and confirm the condensate is draining (portable units either evaporate it or need a drain). A smell that returns within a day means the pan or coil needs a cleaner.

A gas oven that shuts off shortly after preheat and reignites when the surface burners are clicked points to a weak igniter: it glows but does not draw enough current to hold the gas valve open, so the valve closes; clicking a burner resets the circuit. Watch the igniter during the failure — a dull orange glow instead of bright white confirms it. The igniter is a cheap, common part; the gas valve and thermostat are the next suspects if the igniter glows brightly.

One burner stuck at medium-high regardless of the knob is the burner's infinite switch: a failed switch can feed continuous partial power to that one burner. Turn the breaker off and inspect the switch wiring for a short; the switch itself is the part to replace, and it must match the burner's wattage. If the burner stays hot with the knob off, the switch is welded or shorted and must be replaced before further use.

A dryer that spins but never heats, with the timed-dry knob advancing but auto-dry not, points to the heating circuit: the thermal fuse first (the #1 cause of spins-but-no-heat; it sits on the blower housing and kills heat while leaving the motor running), then the heating element and the thermostats; auto-dry not advancing adds the moisture sensor to the list. Test the thermal fuse for continuity, then the element and each thermostat, and check the sensor contacts.

A dishwasher that fills, heats, and drains while the wash pump never runs — relay clicks, no hum, no fault codes — points to the pump motor, the relay or control board driving it, or the wiring to the pump: the control thinks it ran. With power off, check the pump connector for corrosion and the pump motor for continuity; an open motor means a pump replacement, a good motor means the relay or board. The clicking relay with a dead motor is the key symptom.

Both elements dead with controls and light working is almost never two elements at once: it is a lost 240 V leg (120 V still runs controls and lights but heats nothing), a failed oven relay on the control board, or the elements' wiring. Check the breaker (a half-tripped breaker kills one leg) and measure the outlet voltage (200-240 V). If voltage is right, an appliance tech should check the relay and element wiring; if a leg is dead, an electrician is the right call. The diagnosis is knowledge; the fix is a part or a circuit repair.

A thermal fuse that blows every few months with a clear exhaust and a good element points to what the fuse is protecting against: on an outdoor dryer, ambient heat and lint ingress, or a failing thermistor reading high and driving the heater until the fuse opens. Verify exhaust airflow under load, check the thermistor's resistance against the measured 61-71C, and confirm the machine is rated for outdoor use — an indoor-rated dryer in sun will overheat. The fuse is the messenger, not the fault.

Error E64 means the control sees an open heater circuit; a dryer that heats fine for ten to twenty minutes and then throws E64 has a connection that opens when hot: a failing heater terminal (thermal expansion breaking a marginal crimp), a cracked element (passes cold, opens hot), or a failing thermal cutout. Check the heater terminals for heat discoloration and retorque them; test the element cold and remember a cracked element can pass cold. Clean connections point to the heater assembly.

Orange flames with soot on every propane appliance, a backfiring generator, and two regulators already replaced points to the supply itself: bad propane, a still-faulty regulator or second stage, or a leak drawing air into the line. Stop using the appliances (soot means incomplete combustion and a CO risk) and ask the propane company for a gas-quality test, simultaneous pressure readings at every appliance, and a leak-down test with the system pressurized and isolated. Appliance-level fixes cannot address a problem the generator shares.

Lights on but no compressor or fan sound at all means the compressor is not starting: the start relay or overload (most common, especially after years in storage), a seized compressor, or rarely a stuck defrost timer. A full condensation tray says it ran and defrosted. Unplug, check the relay on the compressor (a rattling relay has loose guts), and the overload; if the compressor hums but does not start, the compressor may be seized. After long storage, oil settles and relays stick — replace the relay before condemning the compressor.

A fridge light that only comes on when the freezer door opens means the door-switch wiring is crossed: the freezer switch is wired into the fridge light circuit, or the two switches' leads are swapped. Check the wiring at both door switches against the diagram; this is a wiring job, not a part. If the wiring is correct, one switch's contact is cross-conducting and should be replaced. It is a low-voltage repair once the panel is off.

Oven bulbs burning out every week or two across several brands points to heat or voltage: a loose socket contact (arcing kills bulbs), a bulb not rated for oven use, or high supply voltage. Check the socket for a loose or corroded contact (wobble the base), confirm replacements are oven-rated (not LED unless the oven says so), and measure the supply voltage at the outlet — over about 125 V kills bulbs. A loose socket contact is the most common cause of rapid bulb death.

Error 4U00 on a Bosch hob right after wiring means the hob detected an installation fault: the 5-wire connection is wrong (terminal mapping, phase, neutral, or earth), the supply does not match the hob's rating, or a connection is loose or a strand is shorting between terminals. Turn the power off and re-check the wiring terminal-for-terminal against the hob's diagram, confirm the supply voltage and phase arrangement match the rating plate, and inspect for stray strands. The manual's 4U00 entry names the exact fault; a mis-wired terminal is the most common cause.

Outlets that die or a breaker that pops when a microwave runs points to an overloaded or damaged circuit: the microwave's 1000-1500 W draw on a shared circuit, or a loose or damaged connection in the flipped house's wiring (a bad neutral is the classic — outlets die and breakers pop under load). Move the microwave to a different circuit and test; check the outlet's wiring (back-stabbed connections are a common failure in flipped houses) and the breaker itself. If it follows the microwave, the microwave is the fault; if it stays on the circuit, the wiring or breaker is.

A breaker that is hot to the touch and pops when the oven calls for full heat is most likely failing itself: a weak contact heats and trips under load, and the stove is probably fine. Have an electrician replace the breaker and check the wire torque at its terminals (a loose wire heats the breaker the same way). If a new breaker still pops at high heat, then the oven's element or wiring is shorting — but a hot breaker is the breaker's own signature.

Hollow, shell-like ice cubes are the signature of low water pressure to the ice maker or a faulty water inlet valve: the mold does not fill before the freeze cycle ends. Check the supply valve is fully open and the line is not kinked, and clear the inlet valve's screen; if a sink tap on the same line runs weakly, house pressure is the cause. If pressure is good at a tap, the inlet valve is the likely fault. A too-warm fridge or a mis-level fridge can also make hollow ice, but pressure is the first check.
